record.paper_title: Geodesic Nets: Some Examples and Open Problems
record.original_question: Construct a finite connected irreducible geodesic net in the Euclidean plane with exactly four unbalanced vertices and more than 16 balanced vertices, or prove that no such net exists. The net must have distinct straight-line edges that meet only at common endpoints, satisfy the zero-sum unit-tangent balancing condition at every balanced vertex, and be irreducible in the sense that no proper subset of its edges, together with all vertices incident to those edges, forms a geodesic net with the same four unbalanced vertices.

evidence.quote: one can define irreducible geodesic nets on a given set S of unbalanced vertices as geodesic nets such that no subgraph formed by a proper subset of the set of edges (with all incident vertices) is a geodesic net with the same set S of unbalanced vertices.
Problem 3.2.1. Find an irreducible geodesic net with 4 unbalanced vertices in the Euclidean plane with more than 16 balanced vertices (or prove that such a geodesic net does not exist.)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A finite geodesic net in the Euclidean plane is a finite straight-line graph $G$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose edges are straight line segments meeting only at common endpoints, together with a designated partition of its vertices into "unbalanced" and "balanced" vertices, such that at every balanced vertex $v$ the sum of the unit tangent vectors along the edges incident to $v$ (pointing away from $v$) equals the zero vector. The net is connected if its underlying graph is connected, and irreducible (with respect to its set $S$ of unbalanced vertices) if no proper subset of its edges, together with all vertices incident to those edges, forms a geodesic net having the same set $S$ of unbalanced vertices.

Construct a finite connected irreducible geodesic net in $\mathbb{R}^2$ having exactly four unbalanced vertices and strictly more than sixteen balanced vertices, or prove that no such geodesic net exists.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work (arXiv:2511.07810, "Towards Constructing Geodesic Nets with Four Boundary Vertices and an Increasing Number of Balanced Vertices") reports the construction of an irreducible geodesic net in the plane with 4 unbalanced (boundary) vertices and 25 balanced vertices, surpassing the previous threshold of 16. Thus the existence half of the problem appears affirmatively answered, although no upper bound is established, so the broader question of the maximum number of balanced vertices remains open.

status_evidence.title: Towards Constructing Geodesic Nets with Four Boundary Vertices and an Increasing Number of Balanced Vertices
status_evidence.snippet: A geodesic net in the plane with four boundary vertices and 25 balanced vertices that is irreducible (contains no nontrivial subnets), increasing the previously known number from 16 to 25.
status_evidence.claim: An irreducible geodesic net with 4 unbalanced vertices and 25 balanced vertices has been constructed, exceeding 16.

status_evidence.title: An example for a nontrivial irreducible geodesic net in the plane (Parsch)
status_evidence.snippet: First nontrivial irreducible geodesic net in the plane with 4 boundary vertices and 16 balanced vertices.
status_evidence.claim: The threshold of 16 balanced vertices was the previous benchmark established prior to the problem being posed.
